```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(data.table)
setDTthreads(1)
library(ggplot2)
prefix <- normalizePath(Sys.getenv('CONDA_PREFIX'),mustWork=TRUE)
stopifnot(startsWith(normalizePath(R.home()),paste0(prefix,'/')),
 all(startsWith(normalizePath(.libPaths()),paste0(prefix,'/'))))
for (helper in c('load-set-a','audit-missingness','build-wide','cp2-data',
                 'cp2-preprocess','cp2-models','cp2-run','cp2-plots')) source(paste0('R/',helper,'.R'))

result <- cp2_run()
```

## AI-use statement

I used ChatGPT to plan the modeling and
validation design. I used OpenAI Codex to write and debug the R/Quarto/Pixi
workflow, run analyses and automated checks, inspect figures, and help draft
explanatory text. Automated checks examined data integrity, training-only
preprocessing, cross-validation partitions, event coding, saved predictions,
and reproducible execution. AI accelerated implementation and repeatable testing,
but generated code required debugging. A rendering operation unexpectedly removed
generated output; the submitted CP1 HTML was restored exactly from Git, and
supporting outputs were regenerated with the recorded long/wide hashes checked.
The complete original supporting-output manifest was lost, so full byte-for-byte
restoration of those files cannot be established. The later audit also identified
unstable generalized additive model (GAM) predictions caused by sparse-category
separation. Detailed technical
evidence is recorded in `docs/cp2-verification.md` and `docs/cp2-final-qa.md`.
These automated checks do not establish clinical validity, causality, or
independent external validation.

## 2.1 Modeling table and cleaning

The [PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2012 dataset](https://physionet.org/content/challenge-2012/1.0.0/)
contains intensive care unit (ICU) stays with observations over the first 48 hours.
This analysis uses **Set A only**, with one row per stay. The two windows are
columns: [0,24) and [24,48], so 24:00 begins the second window and 48:00 is included.
All predictors become available only after this 48-hour observation window;
this is not an admission-time prediction system.

```{r}
#| label: cohort
cohort <- data.table(stays=nrow(d$wide),wide_columns=ncol(d$wide),
 deaths=sum(d$y),death_percent=100*mean(d$y),unique_ids=uniqueN(d$ids))
tab(cohort,digits=2,caption='Table 1. Reconstructed Set A modeling cohort.')
```

The reconstructed table has `r nrow(d$wide)` stays and `r ncol(d$wide)` columns,
including `r sum(d$y)` deaths (`r fmt(100*mean(d$y),2)`%). The death indicator is
joined one-to-one by RecordID: source `In-hospital_death` maps to
`In_hospital_death`, with 1 meaning death. Checks require complete binary outcomes,
unique nonmissing IDs, equal patient/outcome ID sets, exact column names,
0–48-hour source times and consistent summary counts. A malformed stay or conflicting
admission descriptor stops construction.

The pipeline reconstructs the wide table directly from `data/set-a/` and
`data/Outcomes-a.txt`. It uses CP1 sentinel (`-1`) handling and hard-invalid
rules in a copied analysis column, preserving original Value and Value_raw.
Hard-invalid rules include negative nonmissing measurements, invalid categorical
codes, and documented bounds for Glasgow Coma Score (GCS), inspired oxygen
fraction, oxygen saturation and pH. CP1 soft zero/extreme flags are retained
unless covered by the prespecified CP2 revision below. Positive maxima are
review flags, not global deletion or winsorization thresholds.

```{r}
#| label: cleaning-summary
cleaning_counts <- data.table(rule=c('CP1 hard-invalid records','CP1 sentinel -1 records',
 'CP2 zero-height records','CP2 zero-weight records'),
 records=c(d$source_summary$hard_invalid,d$source_summary$sentinel_missing,
 sum(d$cleaning$Parameter=='Height'),sum(d$cleaning$Parameter=='Weight')))
tab(cleaning_counts,caption='Table 2. Record-level cleaning counts; different rules may overlap.')
```

CP1 hard-invalid cleaning affects `r d$source_summary$hard_invalid` records.
CP2 additionally sets `r sum(d$cleaning$Parameter=='Weight')` zero-weight and
`r sum(d$cleaning$Parameter=='Height')` zero-height records to missing because
zero body size is not usable. This happens before admission extraction and
window aggregation, so repeated Weight values and valid counts change too.
Other soft flags stay unchanged. Exact changed records, CP1 flags and admission
extraction audits are saved under `output/cp2_*.csv`; CP1 source and generated
results are preserved.

## 2.2 Predictors and eligibility

A positive allowlist supplies **`r length(cp2_predictors())` candidate raw
predictors** to elastic net and random forest: five admission descriptors and
`r length(feature_columns())` summaries (37 variables × two windows × six statistics).
The joined table's 455 columns are not 455 predictors. RecordID, either target
spelling, length of stay, survival, Simplified Acute Physiology Score I (SAPS-I)
and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) are excluded from every model.
Benchmark scores are held in a separate evaluation object.

Gender uses documented categories 0 = female, 1 = male; ICUType uses 1 = coronary
care, 2 = cardiac surgery recovery, 3 = medical ICU, 4 = surgical ICU. Both are
categorical. The dictionary abbreviations are coronary care unit (CCU), cardiac
surgery recovery unit (CSRU), medical intensive care unit (MICU), and surgical
intensive care unit (SICU). Liver enzyme abbreviations are alkaline phosphatase
(ALP), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST).
Other source labels are heart rate (HR), temperature (Temp), respiratory rate
(RespRate), mean arterial pressure (MAP), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and white
blood cell count (WBC). Arterial blood pressure (ABP) uses diastolic (DiasABP)
and systolic (SysABP) labels; NI prefixes identify non-invasive measurements
(NIDiasABP, NIMAP, NISysABP). FiO2 is the inspired oxygen fraction; HCO3 is
bicarbonate; HCT is hematocrit; PaCO2 and PaO2 are arterial carbon-dioxide and
oxygen partial pressures; SaO2 is arterial oxygen saturation; MechVent denotes
mechanical ventilation documentation. Unit IU/L means international units per
liter. A count of zero means no valid measurement, not a measured laboratory
value of zero. Counts can reflect monitoring, treatment decisions and patient
condition; associations are not intervention effects.

```{r}
#| label: predictor-groups
raw_groups <- result$dictionary[model_pool=='Elastic net / forest',
 .(raw_candidates=.N,rationale=rationale[1]),by=group]
encoded_parent <- sub('__.*$','',result$full$enet$preprocess$columns)
encoded_group <- result$dictionary$group[match(encoded_parent,result$dictionary$predictor)]
encoded_counts <- as.data.table(table(encoded_group));setnames(encoded_counts,c('group','encoded_retained'))
groups <- merge(raw_groups,encoded_counts,by='group',all.x=TRUE)
groups[is.na(encoded_retained),encoded_retained:=0]
tab(groups,caption='Table 3. Broad predictor groups and retained full-data encoded columns.')
```

The full-data broad design retains `r length(result$full$enet$preprocess$columns)`
encoded columns. Group counts show the effects of categorical dummy coding and
training-only usability removal; eligibility is otherwise prespecified. No
outcome-driven screening or rare-measurement threshold is used.

<details>
<summary>Complete predictor dictionary: names, windows, definitions and units</summary>

```{r}
#| label: predictor-dictionary
tab(result$dictionary[,.(predictor,group,window,definition,unit)],
 caption='Table 4. All 449 broad candidates plus the GAM-only documentation indicator.')
```

Each name identifies its source, window and statistic; count units are records,
while value summaries keep the original measurement units. TroponinI/TroponinT
are the source-file names corresponding to TropI/TropT in the official definitions.
The additional documentation indicator is GAM-only.

</details>

Within each relevant training partition, a numeric value column is removed if
100% missing; other encoded columns are removed if their sample standard
deviation is zero after training imputation. Useful nonconstant counts remain
even when value summaries are removed. There is no arbitrary rarity cutoff.

```{r}
#| label: dropping-summary
drop_summary <- result$drops[,.(columns_removed=.N),by=.(context,family,reason)]
tab(drop_summary,caption='Table 5. Outer/full-refit column removals under the fixed usability rules.')
```

The table reports removal counts by fit; actual column names and reasons follow
below and are saved in `cp2_dropped_columns.csv`. Inner-partition states and all
inner removals are also saved in `cp2_preprocessing_audit.rds`.

<details>
<summary>Exact columns removed in each outer fit and full-data refit</summary>

```{r}
#| label: dropped-columns
tab(result$drops[,.(context,family,column,reason)],caption='Table 6. Exact dropped columns.')
```

These are training-specific unusable columns, not predictors judged unimportant
from held-out performance.

</details>

## 2.3 Cross-validation and preprocessing

Cross-validation (CV) uses five stratified outer folds by stay, seed **7072026**.
IDs are sorted before seeded assignment; all methods use the identical persisted
outer assignment. Every stay receives exactly one out-of-fold (OOF) probability
from each learned model. The untouched outer fold is predicted only after tuning
and refitting within its outer-training partition.

Elastic net and forest use three stratified inner folds within each outer-training
partition, with seeds 7072026 + outer-fold number. Inner splits are shared across
families and settings. The GAM's fixed formula uses restricted maximum likelihood
(REML) smoothness estimation on outer training; it has no separate CV grid.

```{r}
#| label: fold-layout
fold_layout <- result$oof[,.(stays=.N,deaths=sum(outcome),death_percent=100*mean(outcome)),by=outer_fold]
tab(fold_layout,digits=2,caption='Table 7. Common outer-fold layout.')
```

Every fold contains deaths and survivors. Each validation stay is excluded from
both its outer-training fit and all associated inner folds; the checks also
verify complete, nonoverlapping assessment coverage.

Preprocessing is fitted separately in **every inner training split**, again on
the whole outer-training partition after tuning, and finally on all Set A for
refits. Numeric measurements use training medians. For each categorical predictor,
training-observed categories define the levels, plus a missing level when training
has missing values. Missing/unseen categories map to that missing level if present;
otherwise they map to the training mode (ties choose the lowest code). Dummy coding
omits the first training-observed level as reference. These rules never learn levels
from validation data and never silently discard rows.

Elastic net explicitly centers and scales every retained column, including binary
and dummy columns, by training mean and sample standard deviation. `glmnet` then
uses `standardize = FALSE`; its coefficients are therefore on this explicit standard deviation (SD)
scale. GAM and forest retain original measurement units. GAM counts are prespecified
`log1p(count)` parametric terms. Counts are complete measurements of record frequency,
not missing values needing imputation.

Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) always defines
1 = death and larger probability/severity score = greater risk. No automatic receiver operating characteristic (ROC)
direction selection is used. The main summary is the unweighted mean and sample
standard deviation (SD) of five fold AUROCs. The OOF ROC plot also reports pooled
AUROC, which is a different summary.

Nested tuning limits hyperparameter-selection leakage. **Choosing the winning
family using the same outer-CV results can still make its reported performance
optimistic**. This is internal evaluation, not independent external validation.

## 2.4 Model 1: Elastic-net logistic regression

Binomial elastic net uses fixed alpha = 0.5, a compromise between sparse selection
and shrinkage of correlated summaries. Lambda is tuned over 30 descending
log-spaced values from 1 to 0.0001. Selection maximizes mean inner-fold AUROC;
ties within `1e-10` favor the larger lambda. The complete fixed path is fitted
with 100,000 maximum passes; convergence and path coverage are checked. The grid
is not expanded in response to outer-fold scores.

```{r}
#| label: enet-tuning
tab(result$hyperparameters[family=='enet',.(context,design_p,lambda,boundary)],digits=6,
 caption='Table 8. Chosen elastic-net penalties and boundary selections.')
```

The all-Set-A interpretation fit uses lambda
`r fmt(result$full$enet$hyperparameters$lambda,6)`, selected using fresh three-fold
CV on all Set A (seed 7072926). Boundary selections are explicitly reported above.
Full tuning results are saved in `cp2_tuning_enet.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-coefficients
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Largest standardized elastic-net coefficients in the all-Set-A fit."
plots$coefficient
```

The fit retains `r sum(result$coefficients$retained)` nonzero design coefficients
using tolerance `1e-8`; the figure shows the 25 largest absolute coefficients,
excluding the intercept. A coefficient is the conditional log-odds change per
training SD of its encoded predictor. For a dummy, one SD is not a complete
category change. The largest absolute coefficient belongs to
`r result$coefficients[order(-abs(standardized_coefficient)),predictor][1]`.
These are predictive associations, not causal effects or biological discoveries.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stability
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Predictor retention across the five outer-training elastic-net fits."
plots$stability
```

`r sum(result$stability$retained_folds==5)` predictors are retained in all five outer
fits; `r sum(result$stability$retained_folds>0)` appear in at least one. The figure
shows the 25 highest-frequency predictors, breaking display ties by absolute
full-fit coefficient. Correlated first/last/extreme/window summaries can substitute
for each other, so unstable selection need not imply an absent biological
association. Ordinary elastic net does not enforce selection of a whole factor.

<details>
<summary>All encoded coefficients and retention in each outer fold</summary>

```{r}
#| label: full-coefficients
tab(result$stability[,.(predictor,standardized_coefficient,retained,
 fold_1,fold_2,fold_3,fold_4,fold_5,frequency)],digits=5,
 caption='Table 9. Full coefficient table and outer-fold retention; absent fold columns count as unretained.')
```

The complete table makes truncation in both figures explicit and allows checking
whether full-fit retained predictors recur across folds. No post-selection Wald
intervals are supplied.

</details>

## 2.5 Model 2: Logistic GAM

The GAM uses 17 clinically prespecified source variables, rather than features
selected using every validation label: age, Gender, ICUType, second-window mean
heart rate, temperature, mean arterial pressure (MAP) and respiratory rate; minimum
GCS; last creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), white blood cell count (WBC),
platelets and lactate; documented mechanical ventilation; and MAP, creatinine and
lactate counts. This represents demographics, observed physiology, labs, treatment
documentation and monitoring intensity. It does not assert 17 independent causal
risk factors.

```{r}
#| label: gam-inputs
tab(result$dictionary[match(cp2_gam_variables,predictor),.(predictor,window,unit,rationale)],
 caption='Table 10. Prespecified GAM source-variable set.')
```

Categorical terms use the same training-defined dummy rules; continuous terms use
`k = 5` basis dimensions with REML smoothness estimation. Counts enter linearly
on the log1p scale, and documentation is binary. If a continuous variable has
fewer than five distinct imputed training values it is linear; an unusable or
constant column is dropped. The source-variable count is separate from the
`r length(result$full$gam$preprocess$columns)` retained encoded inputs and
`r length(coef(result$full$gam$model))` fitted regression/spline coefficients.

The ventilation indicator equals 1 when any valid MechVent = 1 is documented in
24–48 hours. Zero means no such documentation, not proof of no ventilation.
Its full-cohort documented count is
`r sum(d$x$MechVent_h24_48_documented_1)` stays. Median imputation is a practical
way to retain rows, but may blur physiology when measurements are selective.

The following all-Set-A smooths show **centered contributions to the log odds**,
with approximate 95% pointwise bands and rugs for observed, nonimputed values.
Zero is a centering constraint, not a clinical threshold, absolute probability
or odds ratio. The bands are conditional on this formula and imputation procedure;
they do not capture all selection, missing-data or modeling uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gam-age
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Age smooth: centered log-odds contribution, pointwise band and observed support."
plots$effects[[1]]
```

For age, effective degrees of freedom (EDF) are
`r fmt(plots$effect_summary[variable=='Age',edf],2)`. The fitted centered contribution
at the 10th, median and 90th observed percentiles is respectively
`r paste(fmt(unlist(plots$effect_summary[variable=='Age',.(contribution_q10,contribution_median,contribution_q90)])),collapse=', ')`.
The age contribution increases almost linearly over the observed range; EDF about
one provides little evidence of nonlinearity in this fit. This is consistent with
older age being associated with higher mortality conditional on the other inputs,
without attributing an intervention effect to age. Bands widen toward younger and
older extremes, so the fitted slope has less precision there.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gam-hr
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Second-window mean heart-rate smooth in original beats/min units."
plots$effects[[2]]
```

Heart-rate EDF is `r fmt(plots$effect_summary[variable=='HR_h24_48_mean',edf],2)`.
The fitted contributions at the 10th, median and 90th percentiles are
`r paste(fmt(unlist(plots$effect_summary[variable=='HR_h24_48_mean',.(contribution_q10,contribution_median,contribution_q90)])),collapse=', ')`.
The fitted association increases across the observed range, with modest upward
curvature rather than a U-shape. EDF about 1.63 suggests limited nonlinearity,
weaker than for temperature. Higher heart rate can plausibly summarize
physiological stress, but treatment and case mix may contribute to this
association. Sparse low/high values have wider bands, limiting tail interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gam-temp
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Second-window mean temperature smooth in original degrees C, zoomed to the observed 1st–99th percentile range; no observations are removed from fitting."
plots$effects[[3]]
```

Temperature EDF is `r fmt(plots$effect_summary[variable=='Temp_h24_48_mean',edf],2)`.
The fitted contributions at the 10th, median and 90th percentiles are
`r paste(fmt(unlist(plots$effect_summary[variable=='Temp_h24_48_mean',.(contribution_q10,contribution_median,contribution_q90)])),collapse=', ')`.
The central supported range shows a declining contribution toward a trough near
37.5 degrees C, followed by an upturn at higher temperatures. EDF about 3.39
indicates more curvature than age or heart rate. This pattern is compatible with
temperature departures marking illness, but it is an adjusted predictive
association. The main view zooms to the observed 1st–99th percentiles; all
observations remain in fitting. The full-range curve below has a poorly supported
low-temperature downturn, so a simple U-shape must not be asserted over the entire
range. Sparse tails, retained soft concerns and wide bands limit clinical reading.

<details>
<summary>Temperature smooth over the full observed range</summary>

```{r}
#| label: fig-gam-temp-full
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Untrimmed temperature range: very sparse low-temperature observations produce large uncertainty."
plots$temperature_full
```

The untrimmed curve shows why low-temperature extrapolative-looking shapes need
caution: its far-left band is much wider than in the densely observed central
range. The displayed zoom changes only the view, not the data or fitted model.

</details>

```{r}
#| label: smooth-support
tab(plots$effect_summary[,.(variable,observed_n,imputed_n,minimum,q10,median,q90,maximum,edf)],digits=2,
 caption='Table 11. Observed support and fitted EDF for the three displayed smooths.')
```

The support table quantifies how many original observations versus imputed values
underlie each fit. The observed range is shown without global winsorization;
less-supported ranges should carry less interpretive weight.

<details>
<summary>Convergence and basis-adequacy diagnostics</summary>

```{r}
#| label: gam-diagnostics
tab(result$gam_diagnostics,digits=3,caption='Table 12. GAM basis checks for outer fits and all-Set-A refit.')
```

All fitted GAMs must pass convergence checks. Basis checks use a fixed diagnostic
seed and 200 permutations. Low k-index p-values, especially with EDF near `k - 1`,
can indicate inadequate basis size; the prespecified formula is not retuned using
outer scores. Binary-outcome residual checks and multiple checks warrant caution.
In this run, full-fit basis p-values are all above 0.05, although temperature EDF
(3.39 of at most 4) merits attention. Some outer fits have low p-values for BUN
and lactate, including 0.005 for lactate in fold 5; their EDFs are well below 4.
These diagnostics remain a methodological limitation rather than grounds for
outcome-guided formula revisions. Exact formula/fallback records are saved in
`cp2_gam_terms.csv`.

</details>

Three incorrect extreme OOF GAM probabilities—one death near zero and two
survivors near one—were driven by the unpenalized dummy for missing Gender.
That category had only one or two outer-training stays, all with the same outcome,
in the affected folds. This produced quasi-complete separation and very large
coefficients despite convergence checks passing. The frozen model and AUROC
comparison are retained. This is a sparse-category stability and individual-risk
limitation, rather than an established input or event-coding defect. The category
coefficient does not establish a causal effect, and saturated fitted probabilities
must not be equated with reliable clinical risks or clinical certainty.

## 2.6 Model 3: Probability random forest

The `ranger` probability forest uses the same 449 broad candidates, training-only
median imputation, categorical dummy encoding and usability dropping. It does not
scale numeric columns. Predictions explicitly extract the column named `1`
(death), not the survival column. Out-of-bag performance is not used for the
required common-fold comparison.

The fixed grid has 500 trees, mtry rules `floor(sqrt(p))` and `floor(p/3)` (bounded
to [1,p] and deduplicated within each training design), and minimum node sizes
5, 20 and 50. Here p is the retained training design dimension. Settings maximize
mean three-fold inner AUROC; numerical ties favor larger node size, then smaller
mtry. Bootstrap sampling with replacement uses fraction 1, Gini splits, one thread,
fixed seeds and no early stopping. Missing values are explicitly imputed and the
forest uses `na.action = 'na.fail'` as a safeguard.

```{r}
#| label: forest-tuning
tab(result$hyperparameters[family=='forest',.(context,design_p,mtry_rule,mtry,node)],
 caption='Table 13. Selected forest settings from training-only tuning.')
```

The table shows which prespecified settings were chosen in each outer fit and,
if selected as final family, the full-data tuning fit. Full grid results are
saved in `cp2_tuning_forest.csv`. A training-only 500-tree smoke test took 10.605
seconds on this development machine before outer evaluation, supporting the
original grid; this is a recorded development measurement, not a claim about
runtime on every laptop.

## 2.7 Benchmarks, comparison and final model

SAPS-I and SOFA are used **alone as raw severity scores**, not fitted models,
model predictors or calibrated probabilities. Their documented `-1` codes map
to missing in evaluation copies. No logistic calibration or outcome-based
benchmark imputation is performed.

```{r}
#| label: benchmark-availability
bench_counts <- data.table(score=c('SAPS-I','SOFA'),
 available=c(sum(!is.na(result$oof$SAPS_I_score)),sum(!is.na(result$oof$SOFA_score))),
 missing=c(sum(is.na(result$oof$SAPS_I_score)),sum(is.na(result$oof$SOFA_score))))
tab(bench_counts,caption='Table 14. Benchmark availability among all Set A stays.')
```

The primary five-method comparison uses the same `r sum(comparison$common)`
score-available stays, with `r sum(d$y[comparison$common])` deaths,
in the existing outer folds. `r sum(!comparison$common)` stays lack at least one
benchmark and are excluded from this comparison; every learned-model OOF prediction
is still retained. The availability table makes the evaluation cohort explicit.

```{r}
#| label: five-method-comparison
main <- comparison$summary[,.(Method=method,`Fold 1`=`1`,`Fold 2`=`2`,`Fold 3`=`3`,
 `Fold 4`=`4`,`Fold 5`=`5`,Mean=mean_auc,SD=sd_auc,Stays=n,Deaths=deaths)]
tab(main,digits=4,caption='Table 15. Common-cohort fold AUROCs, unweighted mean and sample SD.')
```

The highest mean AUROC among learned models is for **`r result$selected`**.
These fold values share assessment stays across methods, enabling a descriptive
comparison. They remain estimates from overlapping training populations, not five
independent experiments.

```{r}
#| label: comparison-denominators
tab(unique(comparison$fold[,.(fold,n,deaths)]),
 caption='Table 16. Common comparison denominator and deaths in each outer fold.')
```

These are the denominators behind every method's fold AUROC in Table 15. This
prevents a higher score from reflecting a different benchmark-available population.

```{r}
#| label: fig-five-roc
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "ROC curves for all five methods on aligned OOF predictions/raw benchmark scores."
plots$roc
```

The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves show discrimination over
thresholds on the same stays. Pooled AUROCs in the legend summarize aligned OOF
probabilities and severity scores; they do not replace the mean fold AUROCs in
the main table. Scores are on different scales, so this is not a comparison of
calibrated risks or actionable treatment thresholds.

```{r}
#| label: benchmark-differences
winner_auc <- comparison$fold[method==result$selected,.(fold,winner_auc=auc)]
differences <- merge(comparison$fold[method %in% c('SAPS-I','SOFA')],winner_auc,by='fold')
differences[,difference:=winner_auc-auc]
difference_summary <- differences[,.(mean_difference=mean(difference),
 sd_paired_difference=sd(difference),min_difference=min(difference),max_difference=max(difference)),by=method]
tab(difference_summary,digits=4,caption='Table 17. Descriptive paired fold differences: chosen model minus benchmark.')
```

Compared with SAPS-I and SOFA, the chosen model's mean differences are
`r fmt(difference_summary[method=='SAPS-I',mean_difference],4)` and
`r fmt(difference_summary[method=='SOFA',mean_difference],4)` respectively.
The corresponding paired-difference SDs are
`r fmt(difference_summary[method=='SAPS-I',sd_paired_difference],4)` and
`r fmt(difference_summary[method=='SOFA',sd_paired_difference],4)`.
Here the mean gains over both raw benchmarks are larger than the corresponding
paired-difference SDs and than the individual methods' fold SDs. The improvement
in discrimination is therefore large relative to this observed CV variability,
but this descriptive comparison is not a significance test or evidence of
clinical usefulness. Elastic net exceeds forest by only
`r fmt(comparison$summary[method=="Elastic net",mean_auc]-comparison$summary[method=="Random forest",mean_auc],4)`,
which is small beside their fold variation; that ranking is not persuasive
evidence of superiority.

<details>
<summary>Separate full-cohort learned-model summary</summary>

```{r}
#| label: full-cohort-models
tab(comparison$full_models[,.(mean_auc=mean(auc),sd_auc=sd(auc),stays=sum(n),deaths=sum(deaths)),by=method],
 digits=4,caption='Table 18. Full-cohort learned-model comparison, separate from the common benchmark cohort.')
```

This table retains all learned-model OOF predictions, including stays without a
benchmark. Its population differs from Table 15 only when benchmark scores are missing.

</details>

The final family is **`r result$selected`**, selected by highest common-cohort
mean outer AUROC. Ties within `1e-10` favor elastic net, then GAM, then forest.
The small lead over forest combines with the elastic net's simpler prediction
path and readable coefficients to support this choice;
its ranking alone is not evidence of general superiority. Elastic net provides shrinkage and readable coefficients;
GAM permits visual nonlinear associations; forest permits flexible interactions
but has more tuning/computational cost and less direct interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: final-settings
hp <- result$bundle$hyperparameters
tab(data.table(parameter=names(hp),value=vapply(hp,as.character,character(1))),
 caption='Table 19. Full-data selected-family hyperparameters.')
```

The selected family is refitted on all Set A using its defined three-fold tuning
procedure (or fixed REML for GAM), not an average of outer-fold hyperparameters.
Table 19 gives the actual final settings. All-data elastic net and GAM fits are
also retained for the required interpretation even if the forest wins.

`output/cp2_final_model.rds` contains the fitted estimator, fitted imputation,
category fallback, design order, scaling, hyperparameters, event mapping, seeds,
fold references, package versions and feature-construction specification.
`cp2_predict()` takes a constructed predictor table and uses saved state without
outcomes or re-estimating preprocessing. Saved/reloaded predictions agree within
`1e-12` on a Set-A-derived predictor-only fixture (actual maximum absolute error
`r fmt(fread('output/cp2_reload_check.csv')$max_absolute_reload_error,12)`).

`output/cp2_oof_predictions.csv` stores one row per stay, outcome, outer fold,
three OOF mortality-probability columns and two raw severity-score columns.
Metrics and ROC curves use the newly written OOF CSV as their common evaluation
source, so the displayed comparison can be recomputed from the saved predictions.
OOF values are not replaced by all-data fitted probabilities. Applying this
bundle to another dataset is outside this checkpoint.

## Reproducibility

Run `pixi run --locked checkpoint2` from the repository root with supplied
Set A inputs. No earlier CP1 run, generated CSV, clinical download or personal
R library is required. The report fails on R errors, sets fixed seeds, and
embeds figures/resources. All generated analysis files are written under
`output/`; only rendered reports are versioned among generated outputs.

The actual runtime/machine log is `output/cp2_runtime.txt`; verification commands,
exit statuses, numerical checks and rendering diagnostics are documented in
`docs/cp2-verification.md` and the technical execution record in
`docs/cp2-submission-readiness.md`.

```{r}
#| label: warning-audit
warning_display <- data.table(status=if(length(result$warnings)) 'Captured modeling warning' else 'No R modeling warnings',
 detail=if(length(result$warnings)) unique(result$warnings) else 'Convergence/path checks passed; basis diagnostics are shown separately.')
tab(warning_display,caption='Table 20. Modeling warning audit for this execution.')
```

Warnings are preserved in `cp2_warnings.log`, rather than discarded. The audit
above reports actual modeling warnings from this run; environment warnings and
GAM basis limitations are recorded separately in verification and diagnostics.

```{r}
#| label: session-packages
packages <- c('data.table','glmnet','mgcv','ranger','pROC','ggplot2','knitr','tidyverse')
tab(data.table(package=c('R',packages),version=c(as.character(getRversion()),
 sapply(packages,function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p))))),caption='Table 21. Versions resolved in Pixi.')
```

These are the versions used in this run. Installed package help, including
`glmnet` 5.0's control API, was checked during development; the report does not
claim a development manual proves the installed API. Runtime and changing
machine/date strings are kept out of this version table.
